articles.title_orig: Trump administration orders Commerce to close chip loophole at heart of Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: Trump administration orders Commerce to close chip loophole at heart of Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
President Trump speaks to members of the media on the South Lawn of the White House on Nov. 16, 2026, ahead of a fraught meeting this week with President Xi Jinping of China where A.I. chips could be a key issue.
The Trump administration on Monday announced it was tightening a loophole that has allowed Chinese tech firms to bypass U.S. restrictions on accessing the most advanced A.I. chips through third countries.
The move comes just days ahead of President Trump’s meeting this week with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and in the wake of Nvidia, the creator of the most advanced AI chips, becoming enmeshed in an international scandal that prompted the resignation of CEO and President Jensen Huang and a fresh round of scrutiny over the company’s ties to China.
The new rule released by the Commerce Department will require that buyers of advanced semiconductors from certain countries will need to secure a license to sell or transfer those chips.The administration said the rule would specifically impact buyers from Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, describing those countries as having a “higher than normal” risk of evading current sanctions.
The measure is set to go into effect in 90 days.
China is currently barred from purchasing certain advanced chips directly from U.S.-based companies like Nvidia. Yet some Chinese companies have circumvented the rules by either purchasing the chips through shell companies in third countries, or renting computing powers among data centers located in countries where the U.S. hasn’t restricted on chip exports.
The new rule will also give Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wide discretion as to which chips may require more safeguards. According to the rules, the secretary may inform a company selling AI chips “orally” about stricter export rules on certain items if the department believes there is “an unacceptable risk.”
The rules came days after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Lutnick for failing to properly oversee the chip exports to China in a CNBC interview on Sunday.
The rare public criticism came after Huang’s resignation as head of Nvidia in the wake of revelations about his extramarital affairs, including a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected by the Commerce Department of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls, but a month-long investigation by the Commerce Department into Megaspeed was halted last year after a top Nvidia official intervened , according to the New York Times.
“Treasury, War, USTR and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent said on CNBC on Sunday. “But Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.”
“President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage,” Bessent added.
Both Lutnick and Bessent are expected to travel with Trump to China this week, according to Semafor. Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Aside from AI chips, the first-of-its-kind summit will also focus on the reduction of nuclear weapons.
The federal government began restricting China's access to AI chips in Trump's first term, as both countries raced to become the leader  in this fast-evolving technology. The Biden administration intensified this policy , making the export of advanced chips to China illegal in 2022. Beijing nevertheless still succeeded in stockpiling thousands of chips to build its own AI systems thanks to an international smuggling network.
Last year, Trump reversed his own administration’s export restrictions, allowing Nvidia to sell two types of computer chip used in the development of artificial intelligence to "approved customers" in China in exchange for a portion of the revenue cut. Those moves are poised to draw more scrutiny next year when Democrats take control of Congress, with both chambers likely probing the Trump Administration's AI policies in the wake of the Nvidia scandal. Congressional lawmakers have asked the Commerce Department to preserve all records related to Nvidia as a part of the investigation.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls more than 2%, extending slide to third day as Nvidia drags down AI trade
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls more than 2%, extending slide to third day as Nvidia drags down AI trade
articles.content_orig:
Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , the tech industry is under mounting strain.
Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market.
With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon , whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic's spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI, are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process.
Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus . It's on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google , though delivery won't start until 2028.
"The numbers are just staggering," Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. "It's hard to get your head wrapped around it."
Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips.
By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic's $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments.
The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.
"Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract."
Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future.
"In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus.
Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment.
It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.
Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds , which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.
Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress , who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.
The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech's heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.
Google will be paying particularly close attention.
The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab's $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf , which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said .
"Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google," said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.
Google didn't provide a comment.
One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.
"You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business," said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. "It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world."
Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America , Blackstone , Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion .
That's a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that's never lived through a technology downturn.
"It's not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing," said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. "They're investing, in a sense, in themselves. They're putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action."

articles.title_orig: U.S. Soybean Farmers Push Trump to End China's 10% Tariff Ahead of Xi Meeting
articles.title_zh: U.S. Soybean Farmers Push Trump to End China's 10% Tariff Ahead of Xi Meeting
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON, November 16, 2026. - American soybean farmers are urging President Donald Trump to secure the removal of China's remaining 10% tariff on U.S. soybeans ahead of his planned meeting with President Xi Jinping this week. The American Soybean Association (ASA) has warned that the trade barrier continues to undermine U.S. competitiveness against South American exporters, particularly Brazil. The negotiations could shape future agricultural exports, commodity prices and farm profitability across the Midwest, where producers face rising input costs and uncertain international demand.
The ASA has formally pressed Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to prioritize tariff elimination. Growers argue that Chinese purchase commitments alone cannot restore normal commercial access when private importers face additional costs on American soybeans. The tariff encourages Chinese crushers and trading companies to source supplies from Brazil, where exporters can compete without the same trade penalty. For U.S. farmers, restoring market access is essential to rebuilding predictable demand and reducing reliance on government-negotiated purchases.
The USDA has also identified the competitive disadvantage created by China's tariff policy. In its September 2026 oilseeds analysis, the department reported that Chinese commercial buyers were favoring South American soybeans while state-owned companies continued purchasing U.S. supplies under bilateral agreements. This distinction between government commitments and private-sector demand remains central to the dispute. Even substantial state purchases may not guarantee sustained access to China's commercial market, which remains critical for long-term export growth.
USDA export sales figures through November 5 showed approximately 611.3 million bushels of U.S. soybean commitments to China , with an additional reported sale bringing the total close to 616.2 million bushels, or roughly 16.8 million metric tons. That represents about 67% of the proposed annual target of 25 million metric tons. Additional sales listed under unknown destinations could eventually reach China, but their final buyers have not been confirmed. These figures reflect sales commitments rather than completed shipments, an important distinction for evaluating trade progress.
Brazil's position in the Chinese market adds urgency to Washington's negotiations. Chinese importers compare delivered soybean prices, ocean freight, seasonal availability and tariff costs before selecting suppliers. A 10% tariff can significantly influence purchasing decisions , particularly when Brazilian supplies are competitive. For U.S. growers in Iowa, Illinois, Minnesota, Indiana and Ohio, weaker export demand can pressure local cash bids, basis levels and storage decisions, even when domestic yields remain strong.
The broader farm economy also has a stake in the outcome. High machinery, fertilizer, financing and transportation expenses continue to challenge producer margins, making export opportunities increasingly important. Stronger Chinese demand could support grain handlers, agricultural co-ops, rail operators and export terminals , although tariff removal would not automatically guarantee higher soybean prices. Global production, South American harvest conditions, currency movements and USDA supply forecasts would continue influencing the market.
The negotiations also intersect with broader U.S. agricultural policy, including the Farm Bill, crop insurance and farm income protection programs. While the Trump administration argues that tariffs provide leverage in international negotiations, soybean organizations maintain that retaliatory trade barriers create additional uncertainty for producers. The central challenge is turning diplomatic commitments into reliable commercial demand , allowing farmers and agribusinesses to plan beyond short-term political agreements.
With the current trade truce scheduled to run through January 10, 2027, markets will closely monitor any tariff announcement, new Chinese purchasing commitments and subsequent USDA export sales reports. Eliminating the remaining 10% tariff could improve the competitive position of U.S. soybeans against Brazil , but the ultimate impact will depend on actual purchases and shipments. For American agriculture, the Trump-Xi meeting represents more than another round of trade diplomacy: it is an opportunity to rebuild access to one of the industry's most important export markets.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi Meet This Week: Could Footwear See U.S., China Pause Trade Truce Extension a Second Time?
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi Meet This Week: Could Footwear See U.S., China Pause Trade Truce Extension a Second Time?
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.title_zh: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.content_orig:
A nationwide outage impacting Chase banking services led some customers to report trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds.
The outage began Monday morning, and it was unclear how long it would take to resolve, according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
The issues were affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems,” the bank said in statement late Monday. The issue was not “cyber-related,” it added.
The bank said the issue was not systemically impacting the entire banking system. “Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.”
“It is taking longer than usual to service some customers” but all of its customers still have “access to their accounts and funds. We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today.”
The issues at Chase are the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week that have shaken public confidence in systems that tens of millions of Americans use every day. However, there is no evidence that these incidents are connected to one another.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade.
The issues with Chase accounts appeared to be preventing customers from transferring money via Zelle. A representative for the company said that the technical issues on its platform originated with Chase.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” the company told NBC News. “Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds. An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly.”
A representative for U.S. Bank confirmed that Zelle customers were experiencing issues.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted,” the spokesman said. “However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
It was not immediately clear how many Chase accounts were affected by the glitch. The bank counts approximately 94 million customer relationships in the United States, with 5,000 physical branches and 15,000 ATMs.
“This is really retail banking,” and not tied to the rest of JPMorgan Chase, said a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.
Kayla Steinberg is a producer at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue was driven by China last year: report
articles.title_zh: More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue was driven by China last year: report
articles.content_orig:
More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue last fiscal year was generated by China – a massive cut that shows the size of the chip giant’s murky business with the US adversary, according to a report.
Disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang helped power an ecosystem in which it sold its most powerful chips to east Asian data centers that in turn powered tech offered by Chinese tech giants like Alibaba, according to reports.
Such deals drove more than a fifth of Nvidia’s revenue during the previous fiscal year, according to Culper Research, the short-selling firm that originally called out Nvidia’s China issues in May.
Huang’s efforts to supply China with key AI tech showered Nvidia with an eye-watering $12.4 billion in revenue in the six months through July 26 of this year, or 7% of its global revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal, which added that countless more billions of dollars could ultimately trace back to Chinese customers.
The dealings were a workaround to US export controls that sought to keep Nvidia’s top-of-the-line tech out of the hands of Chinese firms – and proved to be a cash cow for the chip giant, according to the Journal report .
As the full extent of Nvidia’s lucrative China business emerges, the Commerce Department announced Monday it is nixing the provision that has allowed Chinese firms to skirt export controls on American AI chips.
Despite US export restrictions that have thwarted US chip sales directly to China, Nvidia sold chips to firms that set up data centers in Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia which then sold the computing power to Chinese tech giants.
Some of those firms – including Singapore-based Megaspeed , which was led by Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy and mistress to the former Nvidia CEO – have even been suspected of forwarding chips directly to China.
Between March 2024 and June 2025, Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion worth of top-of-the-line Nvidia chips to companies in China, according to the WSJ report.
Shipment records show orders for several hundred thousand of the type of chips that US regulations intended to keep out of Chinese hands. The report notes that records don’t specify how many of the chips were actually delivered or where they originated from.
The department’s Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule that seeks to close a loophole that Chinese firms have used to lease Nvidia’s advanced computing power by going through data centers in third-party countries, according to a Monday press release .
A license will now “be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion,” according to the new rule .
In a Sunday letter addressed to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington – the top Dem on the Senate Commerce Committee – urged the Commerce secretary to reinforce export controls on the sale of AI chips to China.
Chinese firms like Alibaba and ByteDance have “used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models,” she wrote. “These companies are exploiting a loophole in US export controls by using advanced American chips in foreign data centers even when those chips are restricted from the [People’s Republic of China].
Nvidia says it works to prevent smuggling.
Megaspeed told the Journal that it conducts lawful business and designs its supply chain to comply with US export controls. Megaspeed added that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it has retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation.
Lutnick has come under fire since the revelations with critics on Capitol Hill questioning why the agency didn’t blacklist Megaspeed. Lutnick – whose job is speculated to be in jeopardy – is set to testify before the Senate about his agency’s handling of AI chip export controls.

articles.title_orig: Defying court order, Energy Department again forces Michigan coal plant to stay open past retirement
articles.title_zh: Defying court order, Energy Department again forces Michigan coal plant to stay open past retirement
articles.content_orig:
This story was originally published by Ottawa News Network.
PORT SHELDON TWP. — The U.S. Department of Energy has issued a seventh consecutive 90-day emergency order keeping the coal-fired J.H. Campbell plant in Port Sheldon Township available to operate through mid-February — despite a recent federal appeals court ruling striking down the original directive.
The new order, issued late Friday, Nov. 13 , took effect Sunday, Nov. 15, and runs through Feb. 12, 2027. It instructs the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, or MISO, and Consumers Energy to maintain the 1,420-megawatt facility’s operational readiness for emergency grid needs while using economic dispatch to limit ratepayer costs.
Operating along the Lake Michigan shoreline since 1962, the 64-year-old plant had been slated to burn its final ton of coal on May 31, 2025 — roughly 15 years ahead of the end of its scheduled design life — under a 2022 state-approved clean energy transition plan expected to save ratepayers roughly $600 million by 2040.
Instead, just eight days before decommissioning, federal officials intervened with the first of several 90-day mandates. Keeping the aging facility running past its planned closure has added roughly $640,000 to $1 million per day in unbudgeted coal deliveries, maintenance and compliance costs, accumulating between $259 million and $295 million in extra expenses as of September 2026, according to federal court filings and estimates from state officials.
Read More: Cost of the Campbell: How a West Michigan coal plant became the epicenter for a U.S. energy war
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in the latest order that keeping dispatchable coal generation active remains necessary to prevent winter blackouts across the region.
“President Trump and the Energy Department remain committed to doing everything in our power to stop power outages for American families and businesses,” Wright said. “Ensuring coal plants such as the Campbell Plant are available to operate has prevented blackouts and likely saved lives. Americans deserve access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity regardless of whether the wind is blowing or the sun is shining.”
According to the DOE, ongoing reliability strains mirror events observed earlier this year. Officials pointed to a joint report from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and the North American Electric Reliability Corporation analyzing the Winter 2026 Arctic Cold Period — including Winter Storm Fern, during which MISO declared energy emergency alerts and Campbell generated more than 201,000 megawatt-hours of electricity.
Before federal officials intervened in May 2025, the debate over the plant’s future played out inside the Ottawa County Board of Commissioners’ boardroom, exposing local political divides over grid reliability and environmental impacts.
As reported by the Ottawa News Network, far-right Ottawa Impact commissioners pushed in early 2025 for the county to sue Consumers Energy to halt the shutdown — and some community members floated having the county take over the facility as a public utility.
While the full board rejected a lawsuit 7-4, commissioners voted 9-1 in February 2025 to approve a nonbinding resolution authored by then-Vice Chair Josh Brugger urging state regulators and the utility to pause the closure and review grid conditions.
“There was a concern by some constituents that the plant was going to close and they wanted it to stay open. There were also concerns by other members of the community who were concerned that it might stay open, and they wanted it to be closed for environmental issues among other things, so that came to the fore very quickly in 2025,” Brugger, who is now the board’s chair, told ONN earlier this year.
Reflecting on the board’s decision to weigh in on state and federal energy policy, Brugger added: “We felt, in the end, that we were kind of closest to the area of concern and so perhaps we had a different perspective. In hindsight, I’m not sure that we did, but that’s what we felt, and we felt we had an obligation to do that.”
Once the federal mandates took effect, frustration across Ottawa County spilled out of meeting rooms and into the streets through a series of rallies and demonstrations.
Ahead of the first 90-day order’s expiration, environmental advocates, medical professionals and local residents — organized by the Michigan League of Conservation Voters and the Sierra Club Michigan Chapter — gathered outside the gates of the Port Sheldon Township facility on Aug. 12, 2025, alongside state Rep. Stephen Wooden, D-Grand Rapids, and former Ottawa County Commissioner Chris Kleinjans.

Read More: Protestors rally in Holland, call for Campbell coal plant to close
Speakers warned about respiratory health risks from sulfur dioxide and particulate emissions, with Grand Haven-area resident Jeffrey Miller telling local media that keeping the plant open made no sense “financially, politically, economically, environmentally.”
Three days later, on Aug. 15, 2025, roughly 100 residents and youth activists assembled at Memorial Park and Window on the Waterfront in downtown Holland, marching to U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga’s district office to demand an end to the federal coal mandate and criticize rising utility costs.
On May 21, 2026 — marking one year since Wright issued the initial emergency order — Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel held a press conference directly outside the Campbell plant to condemn the continued extensions and highlight mounting costs passed on to ratepayers.
The latest federal directive arrives two months after a unanimous panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled on Sept. 11 that the DOE overstepped its statutory authority under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act when it blocked the plant’s May 2025 retirement.
Writing for the court, Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard held that Section 202(c) emergency powers apply only when the agency identifies “a risk of substantial harm from inadequate electricity supply that calls for immediate action by DOE in particular,” rather than long-term resource adequacy concerns managed through state and regional planning.
“Permitting DOE to compel generation in a situation that can be resolved through the ordinary resource adequacy planning mechanisms … would render meaningless the constraints on federal power that Congress imposed throughout the Act,” the court wrote, warning that the department’s interpretation “would empower it to pick its preferred power sources in Michigan — or, presumably, any other state — and order them to operate” and “invites frequent federal interventions that are unsupported by the statute and threaten the stability of the energy market.”
In its Nov. 13 order, the Energy Department noted it has petitioned the D.C. Circuit for a full-court rehearing and continues to invoke its emergency authority.
Michigan officials, health professionals and environmental advocates have sharply criticized the repeated extensions, arguing the orders unlawfully override state regulatory planning while driving up electricity bills and prolonging air and water pollution along the Lake Michigan shoreline. Continued coal combustion emits sulfur dioxide, nitrous oxides and air particulates while adding to coal ash ponds and wastewater discharges that local residents worry threaten groundwater and Lake Michigan.
Nessel, who led the multistate legal challenge alongside environmental groups including the Environmental Law & Policy Center and the Natural Resources Defense Council, said in September that keeping the aging facility open had already cost $295 million.

articles.title_orig: Winter Nightmare Looms Early in Ukraine as Russia Strikes Relentlessly
articles.title_zh: Winter Nightmare Looms Early in Ukraine as Russia Strikes Relentlessly
articles.content_orig:
Raisa Donbekirova, 65, lights an alcohol trench candle, the only source of heat in her apartment, which was left without water, electricity and heating following Russian shelling of critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Jan. 10, 2026. (Andriy Dubchak / Frontliner / Getty Images)
Writer and soldier of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Winter began this year in August, once again confirming that the wisest person in my family was my grandfather Stepan.
He taught me that summer ends on Aug. 2, the feast day of Saint Elijah, according to the old church calendar. From his lessons, I learned that after that day, it is no longer advisable to swim in rivers and lakes because the water in their underwater channels becomes icy cold.
"Elijah pissed in the water," goes a Ukrainian folk saying. Ever since childhood, Elijah has held a special place in my imagination, because you truly have to be a saint to piss cold.
But there are advantages, too: when the weather turns cold, snakes burrow into the ground to hibernate, making it safer to go mushroom picking.
In the Donbas posadkas — the treeline areas where not just acacias, ash, and wild apricot trees grow, but also broad-canopied oaks — my instincts from the Carpathians had me peering under leaves and into the brush all summer, always on the lookout for mushrooms.
This summer, no mushrooms grew in the tree lines near the front because an unprecedented drought had taken hold.
There was a shortage not only of rain but also of the dew that forms before dawn. During the day, even in the shade, it was so hot that your head would spin. Under layers of uniform and body armor, your body heated up from within to the point where you felt sleepy all the time.
"And although the Donbas saw little rain this year, fire kept falling from the sky without pause."
There were no mushrooms, but the hornets made up for their absence. You have to be just as wary of their nests as you are of enemy weapons.
Posadkas , those narrow strips of woodland running through the fields, are a defining feature of the Donbas. They were planted on a massive scale after World War II to protect arable land from hot, dry winds and erosion.
A few rows of trees, barely thirty feet wide, were meant to transform the nature of the steppe. After 2014, they transformed the nature of warfare, too: they became defensive lines, shelters, places where tree canopies give people a chance to survive shelling.
The prophet Elijah is a fitting figure for this year's drought, which plagued all of Europe but exhausted Ukrainian soldiers in the east more than anyone else.
According to the Bible, the prophet lived in the wilderness and ate what ravens brought him. After carrying out God's instructions, he prayed for rain, and eventually a downpour began, accompanied by thunder and lightning.
In Eastern Christianity, Elijah is known as the thunder-wielder who rides across the heavens in a chariot and hurls fiery arrows. And although the Donbas saw little rain this year, fire kept falling from the sky without pause.
It is astonishing how the most modern and technologically advanced war on the planet ultimately depends on nature.
Every drone, from the smallest to the largest, is first and foremost a bird, subject to the laws of aerodynamics and the wind. If the wind is too gusty or too strong, a drone loses its effectiveness or cannot fly at all. Every military shift begins with checking the weather forecast. It is not enough to wet your finger and figure out which way the wind is blowing. You need to know its speed at 100 meters (328 feet) and above.
"We have drones, satellite communications, live video feeds, and artificial intelligence, yet war still comes down to the rhythm of natural cycles."
Cloudy weather reduces the effectiveness of aerial reconnaissance, allowing greater freedom of movement on the ground.
Low fog provides cover for enemy infantry infiltration, but it also allows us to evacuate wounded soldiers quickly.
Mud underfoot makes it impossible for vehicles to move, while freezing temperatures critically affect launch mechanisms and battery life.
A camera may have extraordinarily high sensitivity and still simply fog up because of the temperature change after a drone takes off. Propellers coated with moisture from the fog ice over at altitude.
We have drones, satellite communications, live video feeds, and artificial intelligence, yet war still comes down to the rhythm of natural cycles.
The full-scale invasion probably began on Feb. 24 for two reasons: immediately after the Winter Olympics in Beijing ended, so as not to antagonize China , and to ensure there was enough time before the spring thaw. After all, tanks and heavy armored vehicles, now symbols of a bygone era of warfare because of their failures, needed to cross hard, frozen ground.
Now, on the eve of the fifth winter of the war, the latest technological developments and deadliest weapons are once again being deployed to amplify nature's effects.
At the front, the weather can be an ally or an enemy, a factor that must be taken into account. But behind the lines, Russia is trying to make it part of its own strategy.
When missiles and drones deliberately destroy energy infrastructure, the cold becomes an extension of the attack, one that does not end with the explosion. It lingers in homes, hospitals, and apartments where people try to keep their children warm.
This pushes exhausted civilians toward surrender because the soldiers at the front are not giving up.
On a subconscious level, Russia has always been associated in my mind with winter, snow, and cold.
Winter is Russia's weapon; cold is its immanent essence. Unable to achieve success on the front line, Putin seeks to turn Ukraine's rear into a terrifying winter wasteland. Cut off electricity, water, and heating, and, by this diabolical means, if nothing else, turn Ukraine into the Siberian taiga over the coming months.
"He wants exhausted people, stripped of hope, to finally say: enough already, let's surrender. We no longer have the strength to endure these constant ordeals."
In the hands of this Satan, winter becomes a means of psychological occupation.
What does winter look like in a city that is bombed every day, with power plants, water pumping stations, and heating pipelines deliberately targeted for destruction? An apartment, even the finest one, turns into the Lascaux cave.
Without electricity or gas, the only way to heat it may be to light a fire in the middle of the room. Without running water, living on the 12th floor means you cannot even wash your face, let alone use the toilet.
Imagine what life under these conditions would be like, especially for children and older people.
The terror inflicted on the civilian population of Ukrainian cities is such an obvious war crime by Putin that it is shameful to see people who, at the same time, are willing to shake his hand, lift sanctions, or sign agreements with him.
I am not talking only about real estate brokers and businesspeople across the ocean. There is a whole line of people in Europe waiting their turn, too, hands outstretched.
Every new war crime strengthens their political positions because it instills fear in voters and fuels their desire to escape this reality by hiding behind deceptive populist slogans.
Enough! That word marks the end of summer and the turn toward winter. Enough movement, enough work in the fields. Go back to your warm house and settle into hibernation, nature tells us. Putin listens carefully, taking the warmth away from people's homes. He wants exhausted people, stripped of hope, to finally say: enough already, let's surrender. We no longer have the strength to endure these constant ordeals.
The fifth winter of the great war in Europe once again confronts us with the same question. Unable to achieve decisive victories on the front, Russia is trying to turn life itself into a weapon: warmth, water, electricity, the ability to keep a child warm, and make it

articles.title_orig: Germany, EU states open talks on Rwanda deportation scheme
articles.title_zh: Germany, EU states open talks on Rwanda deportation scheme
articles.content_orig:
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 .
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries .
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

articles.title_orig: US Moves to Curb Remote Access to Nvidia’s Advanced AI Chips
articles.title_zh: US Moves to Curb Remote Access to Nvidia’s Advanced AI Chips
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.
The federal government is stepping up scrutiny of semiconductor exports to ensure that such shipments don't bypass existing regulations prohibiting their sale to certain U.S. competitors, such as China. The temporary regulations follow last week's shock resignation of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company.
Huang's exit has heightened concerns that China and other nations could access Nvidia's advanced chips by renting computing resources through data centers in Southeast Asia.
"The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday. "The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security."
In addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the new rule will require licenses for exporting, re-exporting, or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. BIS said such nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."
The interim rule notes that advances in cloud computing have made it easier for foreign nations to access American AI computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers in countries not subject to U.S. export restrictions.
The Commerce Department wants to "ensure that computing power, based on U.S. technology located in foreign data centers, is not used in a manner contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests," the rule states.
The rule aims to align remote-access protections with existing controls governing physical access to sensitive American technology, the Commerce Department said.
Existing regulations on chip exports apply only to the most advanced semiconductors. "Selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing," President Trump said in remarks at the White House on Monday.
Mr. Trump is heading to Asia on Monday, where he's expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Chinese officials have said the country was not involved in Huang's affair with the suspected spy.

articles.title_zh: Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain

            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles

The rapid proliferation of hyperscale data centres (HDCs) in the USA—mainly driven by the adoption of artificial intelligence—has raised concerns about this industry’s carbon footprint. We compiled facility-level information on 403 US hyperscale data centres operating between May 2024 and April 2025 and estimated their electricity consumption, electricity sources and attributable CO 2 emissions. Across facility-load scenarios, these HDCs consumed approximately 68–99 TWh of electricity and were associated with approximately 21–31 million metric tons of CO 2 under a location-based, total-output balancing-authority attribution method. Under the central scenario, HDC electricity demand was approximately 82 TWh, corresponding to about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption, and attributable CO 2 emissions were approximately 25.7 Mt. Roughly 54% of attributed generation was supplied by fossil-fuel sources. The HDC electricity-weighted total-output carbon intensity was approximately 314 gCO 2 kWh −1 , compared with a US total-output average of approximately 348 gCO 2 kWh −1 . Our approach provides a facility-resolved attributional framework for assessing the carbon footprint of hyperscale data centres using plant-level electricity-generation and emissions data.

Access to the restricted facility-level dataset may be considered for approved research collaborations, subject to the underlying data-use agreement, provider authorization and execution of an appropriate data-use agreement. Requests may be directed to the corresponding author. We provide public state- and balancing-authority-level data exports containing the electricity demand, attributable CO 2 emissions, total-output carbon intensity and attributed fuel mix used in the revised analysis. These aggregate exports reflect the central facility-load scenario ( u = 0.58) and the total-output attribution basis used for the headline results. They are available through the public reproducibility repository 46 . The repository exports, rather than the separate visualization interface, constitute the authoritative public data products for the revised analysis. Because the underlying facility data are protected by a data-use agreement, raw facility identifiers, addresses, coordinates and commercially sensitive facility attributes are not publicly released. The complete facility-level map-generation workflow requires authorized access to those inputs. Access to facility-level map coordinates remains subject to provider authorization and the data-use agreement; public aggregate files do not substitute for the restricted facility-level observations. Source data are provided with this paper.
All code used to estimate HDC power capacity, evaluate the capacity model, compute electricity use and emissions, validate public aggregate exports and reproduce manuscript-facing numerical results is publicly available in the public reproducibility repository 46 . A tagged snapshot corresponding to the Round 3 reproducibility materials is available as version v0.3.1-round3-final 47 . The repository contains: (1) the fully specified scikit-learn capacity-model pipeline, including disclosed predictors, preprocessing, effective hyperparameters, software version and evaluation metrics; (2) a non-identifying 403-row synthetic facility fixture with six missing power-capacity values; (3) a deterministic public synthetic split artefact at results/tables/synthetic_validation/splits.json , together with random and grouped validation outputs; (4) REPRO.md , documenting the validation sample, explicit imputation indicator, software versions, restricted-data workflow and emissions-accounting conventions; (5) scripts/reproduce_model.py , which regenerates the public synthetic validation outputs and writes the deterministic split artefact; (vi) the total-output emissions-attribution workflow using EPA eGRID2023 Revision 2; (7) denominator-audit, plant-inventory, public-export, restricted-data and manuscript-output validation scripts and (8) aggregate state- and balancing-authority-level exports used to verify the headline results. The public synthetic and aggregate materials allow external researchers to execute the capacity-model validation workflow, verify the emissions denominator, reproduce headline scenario totals, sum the public regional exports and run the repository tests without access to restricted facility records.

articles.title_orig: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.title_zh: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.
Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.
It created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI rollout, but the BBC has been told Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang.
Meanwhile the Trump administration on Monday said it will further restrict China's ​access to AI chips from companies like Nvidia.
Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".
The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models.
The move came ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jingping.
The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted to China.
The president's comments on Huang came after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.
However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A person familiar with the thinking of Nvidia's board told the BBC its directors are not interested in bringing Huang back to lead the company.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.
"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X.
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

articles.title_zh: iOS 27.3 gives Apple’s Calendar app new design updates
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.3 beta 2 arrived today, most notably giving the iPhone Duo a face unlock feature . The update also includes some design updates for Apple’s Calendar app.
When you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.
Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a new event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom.
This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both important buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.
Additionally, Apple has moved the current month to the top-center of the screen and added the year too. Because the year is now always prominently visible, Apple removed it from the back button in the top-left.
Finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’
You can reference the full side-by-side in the image above. Overall, these are relatively minor changes but they could make a big difference in everyday use.

articles.title_orig: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face, other AI model loss of control
articles.title_zh: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face, other AI model loss of control
articles.content_orig:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a sweeping lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday, alleging the technology giant jeopardized public safety by creating AI models “without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect” people.
The suit centers on a July incident involving hundreds of autonomous AI agents created by OpenAI that attacked computer systems at Hugging Face , a separate AI company. Bonta’s office alleges the attack was “entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight.”
Bonta’s office further alleges the ChatGPT developer’s failure to secure the testing of its models created a “public nuisance” and violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, a broad consumer protection statute.
In response to a request for comment, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the Hugging Face incident. (In the tech industry, “alignment” refers to keeping AI models in line with human instructions and goals.)
“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” Pusateri added. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”
In a statement accompanying Monday’s legal filing, Bonta said California demands “innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company.”
“While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta added.
California’s Unfair Competition Law prohibits businesses in the state from engaging in illegal, unfair or fraudulent practices.
OpenAI claimed responsibility for the Hugging Face hack in a July 21 blog post . The post described how some of the company’s most advanced models had escaped what was meant to be a secure testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face, a developer platform that was acquired by Nvidia in September for nearly $13 billion.
In late August, OpenAI published a full technical report on the incident, which alarmed AI safety researchers and lawmakers in both parties . The company pledged to “strengthen our safeguards” and characterized the Hugging Face attack as a wake-up call for the AI industry.
“We consider this incident a ‘warning shot’ for us and for the world: evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed,” the company said in an Aug. 26 blog post .
Bonta’s office announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face incident in September before serving an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of a wider inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models.
Bonta, a Democrat who was re-elected this month to a second four-year term, secured an $18 billion settlement in a social media addiction lawsuit against Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram.
He also led a coalition of state attorneys general that sued to block Paramount Skydance’s merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Paramount and the states ultimately settled the antitrust challenge and the corporate tie-up went forward.
Daniel Arkin is a senior reporter at NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Chase customers report widespread online banking problems
articles.title_zh: Chase customers report widespread online banking problems
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Chase reports an issue that appears to be causing outages to online and in-person banking services
An issue with Chase banking services led to some customers of that institution and others reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds Monday.
The issues appeared to be affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” Chase said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”
The issues at Chase were caused by a “technical bug, not a cyber issue,” according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
A Zelle representative said that a technical issue on its platform originated with Chase.
“This is a Chase issue,” a Zelle spokesman told NBC News. “You need to speak to them.”
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
The outages were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade .
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Apple is adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — without new hardware
articles.title_zh: Apple is adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — without new hardware
articles.content_orig:
Apple is testing a new iPhone Duo feature that would use the front-facing camera to look at your face for authentication.﻿
Apple is testing a new iPhone Duo feature that would use the front-facing camera to look at your face for authentication.﻿
Apple is working on a face unlock feature for the iPhone Duo that uses the front-facing camera for authentication, and it’s already testing it with the new iOS 27.3 beta released today, as reported by MacRumors . Currently, the only way to unlock the iPhone Duo is by using Touch ID or entering a passcode, which might feel like a step back if you prefer face authentication using the Face ID feature available on other iPhones.
The iPhone Duo’s face unlock feature seemingly has a few caveats, however: it’s only available for the lock screen, you can only use your face for an unlock if you have used Touch ID or input a passcode within 45 minutes, and you can’t use the face authentication for Apple Pay purchases.
iOS 27.3 is set to launch publicly in December, Apple said last month , so should the feature make it to the full release, you may not have to wait too long for it to be officially available.
Apple reportedly wants to add Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo, Bloomberg reports .

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi, Putin to discuss ’world peace’, China says
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi, Putin to discuss ’world peace’, China says
articles.content_orig:
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda, but Trump says denuclearisation, Iran war, trade and Ukraine will be among topics
The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.
The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip.
Many, including the UN secretary general, António Guterres, had hoped the trilateral talks would be used to discuss reductions in nuclear arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.
In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.
China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.
“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said its foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”
The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”
Guterres said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”. However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.
Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.
The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.
after newsletter promotion
China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.
Trump’s remarks that he wanted to discuss Ukraine could stoke fears voiced by the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the trilateral talks could turn into a “Yalta 2, 3, 4 with a redistribution of influence”. Zelenskyy was referring to the 1945 pact between the US, UK and Soviet Union that created spheres of influence in Europe after the second world war.
“Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” Trump said. He also deflected criticism of Putin in his remarks, saying the Kremlin leader could be “a lot tougher” in Ukraine and that he was already “backing down”.
US officials had said Trump was not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.
For Xi, much of the political benefit will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC .
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.
Sari Arho Havrén, of the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X : “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

articles.title_orig: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’
articles.title_zh: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.
Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley and the World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.
Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.
Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”
He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.
“It’s hard to imagine what the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”
OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.
Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.
“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”
Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.
“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”
