articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.content_orig:
In the past week, shares of Nvidia ( NVDA -3.96% ) have been in a downward spiral. News that Jensen Huang has resigned as president and CEO and has been involved in multiple affairs, one of which may involve a Chinese spy, has significantly weighed on the company's valuation.
The stock has fallen so sharply that it is now trading at levels it hasn't been at since June of last year. Given how sudden and significant the sell-off has been, many investors are likely worried that there may still be worse to come. Could the tech stock fall to $100?
Image source: Getty Images.
When things are going well for a stock, the temptation is to assume it'll only continue to do well and rise higher. And when things are going poorly, many investors may fear that things will only get worse. Both outlooks, however, can be incredibly irrational. Sooner or later, the excitement or panic fades, and the stock stabilizes and may even end up going in the opposite direction.
Due to its sharp decline, Nvidia's stock is now trading at around 20 times its trailing earnings. And on a forward basis, based on analyst expectations of future earnings, its forward price-to-earnings multiple is just ten. That's an incredibly low valuation given that the S&P 500 average is a forward earnings multiple of 19.
The stock is already heavily discounted , and for a more significant decline to take place, one that takes it to $100, that would likely require there to be much more negative news around the tech business. And there would also likely need to be an all-out crash in the tech sector.
NASDAQ · As of 2:56 PM ET 11/16/26
The last time Nvidia's stock was at around $100 was after the Liberation Day tariffs were announced in April 2025. Global trade uncertainty weighed on not only Nvidia but the markets as a whole, and unless there's that kind of uncertainty and fear rattling the markets once more, I wouldn't expect Nvidia to fall to those levels anytime soon.
Nvidia is already an incredibly cheap-looking stock to buy given how well it has performed in recent years. Waiting for an even lower price could be risky for investors, because the risk is that it may never reach those levels; buying the stock now may be a much better move than holding out hope that it will fall even further.

articles.title_orig: Warsh Says Fed Is Gaming Out How AI Could Reshape Economy
articles.title_zh: Warsh Says Fed Is Gaming Out How AI Could Reshape Economy
articles.content_orig:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

articles.title_orig: U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow
articles.title_zh: U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow
articles.content_orig:
An armed robot developed by Turkish defense companies is demonstrated at a facility in Duzce, Turkey, on April 29. Omer Urer/Anadolu via Getty Images hide caption
GENEVA — Negotiations on possible rules for the use of lethal autonomous weapons, also known as 'killer robots' are underway at the United Nations in Geneva.
Supporters of controls on autonomous weapons say this week's U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons (or CCW), which meets just once every five years, is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late.
Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, with some experts warning that the world is just months away from having weapons that can choose targets and make the decision to kill autonomously.
In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, with Ukrainian civilians reporting being 'hunted' by drones as they shop or go to school. But these are still controlled remotely by humans.
Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill – and responsibility for that choice – must stay in human hands. Ahead of this week's meeting, the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope have all called for legally binding rules. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that allowing fully autonomous weapons to kill would be 'crossing a moral red line'.
The Red Cross is especially worried that existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – cannot be fully respected by autonomous weapons. War is often chaotic and confusing, and the situation can change rapidly. Under the Conventions, soldiers who are wounded or in the process of surrendering can no longer be targeted.
Georgia Haines, a legal adviser with the Red Cross, worries that autonomous weapons will not be able to distinguish between a soldier who is still fighting, one who is wounded and one who wants to surrender.
'The risk is that, based on the technology we are seeing, they are not able to understand in the same way that a human is the contextual signals. And so the risks are incredibly high that there will be a misidentification of a target.'
Meanwhile, human rights groups warn that the technology behind AI-assisted weapons is becoming increasingly cheap and easy to use. The more it is adopted by the military, the greater the danger of proliferation and its use by terrorist groups or law enforcement agencies in repressive regimes. In theory , a swarm of autonomous drones could be programmed to kill everyone wearing a red sweater, everyone carrying a poster or even everyone speaking a certain language.
Many of the countries now meeting in Geneva take such concerns very seriously. At least 50, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany, are calling for a strict timetable to agree on binding rules governing autonomous weapons.
But among states that are already developing and using semi-autonomous weapons, there is pushback. The United States, Russia and Israel have indicated they are set to oppose legally binding rules, with Washington proposing a five-year timetable to draft non-binding guidelines instead.
The U.S. is traditionally a late adopter of international treaties. It did not ratify the Ottawa Convention on landmines, for example, although it did, over time, stop deploying them and reduce its stockpiles.
Under President Trump, doubts about international law have grown. Washington has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, and just this weekend, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a keynote speech to the Federalist Society, warned against  "quoting laws to men with swords."
The problem for states meeting in Geneva is that U.N. negotiations on limiting specific weapons are supposed to be conducted by consensus. This was achieved in 1995, when countries agreed to a ban on blinding lasers, but other agreements have proved elusive. With landmines, countries frustrated by the delay finally took negotiations outside the U.N. process to create the Ottawa Convention.
This week, there may be a compromise: a longer or even open-ended negotiating period to come up with rules that individual states can adopt as binding or non-binding. For diplomats supporting such a solution, it is a way to ensure at least some progress. For campaigners, it is less than ideal, with one likening it to kicking a very dangerous can down the road.

articles.title_orig: Five EU countries unveil plans for Rwanda deportation hub
articles.title_zh: Five EU countries unveil plans for Rwanda deportation hub
articles.content_orig:
Five European countries announced a plan on Monday that would send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda , an experiment that comes as governments across the continent toughen their stances on migration.
The joint push from Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece was pitched as a way to handle migrants who had no right to stay in Europe but who, for one reason or another, could not or would not return to their home countries.
The project, which is not yet finalized, shows how European leaders’ stance on migration has hardened since the arrivals of 2015-16, when countries like Germany admitted more than a million asylum seekers. With far-right groups like the Alternative for Germany rising in popularity, centrist leaders have gradually taken a less welcoming stance.
“For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system,” Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark, said at a news conference on Monday.
The pilot project is expected to start on a small scale, with perhaps 100 or 200 deportees. Critics are already worried both about the idea of sending people to a nation to which they have no connection, and about the risk that human rights will not be sufficiently protected in Rwanda.
The country has a history of courting migration-related deals.
Britain developed a plan to send asylum seekers there in 2022, though judges in London ultimately ruled the effort unlawful and it was later abandoned. The United States has recently deported people to Rwanda.

articles.title_zh: Trump’s stake in Nvidia grew to as much as $62 million before scandal broke out
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Donald Trump reported trades this year that suggest he has held between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock, disclosures that will likely escalate scrutiny into the president’s relationship to the AI giant and his administration’s oversight of an industry at the center of international scandal.
Financial disclosures, reviewed by The Washington Post, revealed that the president’s Nvidia stakes grew sharply from an estimated $615,000 to $1.3 million at the end of 2024 to as much as $62 million within the last year. The latest filings ​do not capture trades from the past two months, meaning that the values could be even higher.
The disclosures follow Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO after the revelation of his extramarital affair with ‌Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , who is accused of having intelligence ties to Beijing.
White House officials have repeatedly maintained that the president does not personally pick or trade individual stocks and Trump has rejected calls to divest his stock holdings. Trump’s assets are in a trust managed by his children and independent financial managers handle his portfolio, according to the White House.
But enormous growth of the president’s financial stakes in Nvidia are in parallel to the president’s close relationship to Jensen Huang and the administration’s regulatory moves that have opened the door for the company to do business in China. The president has routinely defended his administration against criticism over export controls that appear to have been lucrative for both Nvidia and the president.
Nvidia’s stock is trading at roughly $157.72, down over 3.1 percent on the day, as investors react to Huang’s blockbuster resignation ahead of a third-quarter earnings call scheduled for Tuesday.
The company’s board, however, is not considering bringing him back, according to CNBC.
Huang’s resignation last week followed news of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. U.S. officials have suspected Alice Huang of spying for China, and the Commerce Department had been investigating whether Megaspeed breached U.S. export restrictions.
The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined Alice Huang had been recruited to influence Jensen Huang to push Nvidia toward selling Beijing more of its advanced chips. The Times also reported Jensen Huang’s second affair, with a Nvidia subordinate, moved the company’s board to force him out last week.
Trump, however, appeared to cast doubt on his own administration’s assessment.
“I don’t know that she’s a spy at all. Nobody's proven that,” he told reporters outside the White House on Monday.
“He probably shouldn’t have been doing, on a personal basis, what he did. You know, from — who knows? That's a different story. But nobody's proven that she's a spy. She may not be a spy,” he said.
“Usually what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” he continued, “I don’t know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don’t.”
According to The New York Times , State Secretary Marco Rubio drafted a classified memorandum on Alice Huang’s alleged scheme and had even briefed the president about her suspected activities while the pair were traveling to China on Air Force One in May — months before Jensen Huang’s admission of the affair.
But Trump reportedly brushed the warnings aside and maintained his relationship with the tech mogul, who frequently appeared at the White House and donated $25 million to the president's ballroom project.
Asked on Monday whether he trusted the intelligence that Rubio reportedly provided him, Trump appeared to suggest he thought the reporting was false.
“Who told me that?” he told reporters. “I haven’t heard that.”
Congressional watchdogs are eager to dive into the president’s stocks and his administration’s policies surrounding AI and Nvidia, which include easing Biden-era export restrictions on American AI chips to China in May 2025. That decision opened the door for Nvidia to sell its chips to approved Chinese customers later that year, with a portion of revenue to the U.S. government.
In December, Trump allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced H200 chips to approved customers in China, with 25 percent of the revenue going to the U.S.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this summer whether the government should investigate Trump’s purchase of as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock — just one week before the Commerce Department formalized those export restrictions. Bessent responded by suggesting that Congress should look into banning its own members from stock trading before looking to the White House.
Trump has sought to diffuse tension among his Cabinet officials in wake of the scandal, following reports that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick prevented U.S. oversight on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China.
That reportedly escalated to a Situation Room showdown between Lutnick and Bessent, who appeared to put the blame on the Commerce chief during an appearance on CNBC last week.
The departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all “were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent told the network.
Notably not on that list: Commerce Department.
Trump, however, appeared to acknowledge that Lutnick likely resisted putting Megaspeed — seen as a pass-through to help Beijing evade export controls — on his department’s “Entity List” of firms not allowed to purchase American products.
“He was doing that because you could have — if you didn’t delay it, If you didn’t do something — you could have a blow up with China,” Trump said Monday. “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I’ll make a decision. But I understand very well both sides.”
Republican and Democratic members of Congress, meanwhile, are jockeying for Jensen Huang to testify before several committees.

articles.title_zh: 'A beautiful woman': Trump unsure Nvidia CEO had affair with Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
President Donald Trump said Monday that he would welcome the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia - days after the chipmaker's co-founder was forced out over an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman - and insisted that no one had proven the woman was a spy.
"There's a big group of people that would like him to return," Trump told reporters as he left the White House to travel to Asia ahead of his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin later this week.
“I think having Jensen go back, a lot of people are asking Jensen. They think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea. I recommended Tim Cook, who, as you know, built Apple, I recommended Tim Cook to go and do a job,” Trump continued.
Huang resigned last week after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang — no relation — a businesswoman that U.S. officials have described as a suspected asset of China's Ministry of State Security.
The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined she had been recruited by the spy agency and tasked with influencing Huang to push Nvidia toward selling Beijing more of its advanced chips. The Times also reported Jensen Huang’s second affair, with a Nvidia subordinate, moved the company’s board to force him out last week.
In the days since, allies of the former Nvidia boss have been attempting to rally support for his return with an online petition that has thus far garnered more than 100,000 signatures, including from Nvidia shareholders and employees.
Tesla and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the founder and chief executive of the video game publisher Epic Games , were among major industry figures supporting an open letter calling for his return.
But Nvidia sources told CNBC on Monday that the company’s board is not considering bringing him back and is instead focused on a probe into whether his actions harmed American national security.
Pressed repeatedly on whether he accepted the U.S. intelligence on Alice Huang, Trump questioned it.
"I don't know that she's a spy at all. Nobody's proven that," he said. "He probably shouldn't have been doing, on a personal basis, what he did. You know, from — who knows? That's a different story. But nobody's proven that she's a spy. She may not be a spy."
Trump earlier offered a broader version of the same claim. "Usually what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Trump said. "I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
Asked whether he trusted the U.S. intelligence that the woman was a Chinese agent, and whether Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him so, Trump said he had not heard it.
"Who told me that? ... I haven't heard that. I haven't heard that," he said. "No, I don't know that she is a spy."
The president’s claims do not square exactly with what is publicly known about U.S. officials’ concerns over the affair.
According to The New York Times, Rubio was so alarmed by what intelligence officials were learning about Alice Huang through electronic surveillance that he drafted a classified memorandum on her alleged recruitment and briefed Trump on it aboard Air Force One in May, en route to China.
But Trump brushed aside warnings from Rubio and nonetheless pressed ahead with a relationship that saw Huang become a frequent White House visitor after donating $25 million to the president's ballroom project.
The president defended the decision to keep selling chips to China and brushed aside the suggestion that his closeness to Huang had endangered national security. "It was not put at risk," he said Monday, before pivoting to a claim that the country "is now stronger than ever before."
Trump also dismissed statements from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC last week that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick resisted putting Megaspeed - a China-linked company run by Alice Huang and thought to be a pass-through to help Beijing evade export controls - on his department’s “Entity List” of firms not allowed to purchase American products.
Asked about that, Trump said Lutnick "might have delayed it, but he was doing that because ... you could have a blowup with China."
"One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China. Different views," Trump said, declining to say whether he would replace Lutnick, who is traveling with him to China aboard Air Force One despite the scandal surrounding him and is scheduled to testify on the Nvidia affair before Congress in the next few weeks.
Huang was barred from selling Nvidia's most advanced processors, including its Blackwell line, to China, a restriction Trump defended while playing down its stakes.
"The only thing he was able to sell to China were chips that were sort of obsolete, a little bit like our avionics," Trump said. "Selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing."
The president said he might raise the alleged spying operation with Chinese President Xi Jinping when the two leaders meet on Thursday but would not commit to doing so when pressed by reporters.
"I'll ask him what I want to ask him," he said.

articles.title_orig: Some OLED MacBook Pro Owners Report Eye Strain and Dizziness
articles.title_zh: Some OLED MacBook Pro Owners Report Eye Strain and Dizziness
articles.content_orig:
Some owners of Apple's new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display say they experience eye strain, headaches, and dizziness when using the laptop, with affected users pointing to the screen's brightness-control system as a possible explanation.
A significant number of complaints have appeared on Reddit, X, and the MacRumors forums since the new models launched earlier this month. The discussions on MacRumors include a dedicated PWM thread , a separate owner poll , and comments in the reviews and display-details threads.
On X, one user said trying the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ in an Apple Store for around 30 minutes left them with a severe headache. The user said they had previously struggled with OLED screens before finding newer implementations tolerable, and called for an option to change the Mac's dimming behavior.
A Reddit user described how reading text, especially against a black background, brought on dizziness and nausea. They said their ‌OLED‌ iPad Pro did not produce the same symptoms. In the main MacRumors forum thread , a 16-inch PROLED owner reported a headache and mild nausea that began to ease after switching back to a mini-LED ‌MacBook Pro‌. Another member, posting in the separate poll thread, said they were returning their PROLED laptop for similar reasons after previously having no difficulty with ‌OLED‌ devices.
The suspected issue is pulse width modulation (PWM). An ‌OLED‌ screen produces light through its individual pixels. With PWM dimming, the display changes the time spent at brighter and darker levels during a rapidly repeating cycle. Spending less time at the brighter level reduces the average amount of light reaching the viewer, making the screen look dimmer.
Those fluctuations can occur too quickly to look like an obvious flashing screen, but some people report discomfort with displays that use them. PWM frequency describes how often the brightness cycle repeats. It is different from refresh rate, which is how often the displayed image updates, so a 120Hz ProMotion specification does not tell you the screen's PWM frequency.
Notebookcheck 's testing of the 14-inch PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ recorded 240Hz flickering whenever brightness was set to 99% or lower, with a measured amplitude of 56%. In other words, the light output fluctuated 240 times per second, and the amplitude describes the size of those fluctuations. The publication warned that sensitive users could experience eye strain or headaches due to the specification.
Mini-LED ‌MacBook Pro‌ displays also use brightness modulation, but Notebookcheck measured a much higher frequency of 14,880Hz on the 14-inch M4 Pro model. Such rapid fluctuations are generally less likely to cause discomfort for PWM-sensitive users.
Apple already provides a Display Pulse Smoothing accessibility option on supported iPhones. The setting offers another way to dim the ‌OLED‌ screen at low brightness, although Apple cautions that it can affect display performance under some conditions. macOS does not offer an equivalent control, but Apple could add one in the future.
The OLED MacBook Pro models start at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch version. Apple continues to sell the mini-LED models alongside them.

articles.title_orig: Mini Review: Tanuki: Pon's Summer (PS5) - Easily One of 2026's Most Charming Adventures
articles.title_zh: Mini Review: Tanuki: Pon's Summer (PS5) - Easily One of 2026's Most Charming Adventures
articles.content_orig:
Tanuki: Pon's Summer is a delight — and a finely crafted delight at that.
This is one of the most downright lovable indies I've played in a long time; it's a consistently charming concoction of semi-open world exploration, character stories, and minigames.
You play as the titular Pon, a lazy little tanuki who's tasked with repairing his god's shrine for the upcoming festival. But this is the kind of work that requires cash, and so our unlikely protagonist somehow snags a job at the local post office.
What follows is a day-to-day adventure across a rural Japanese island, where Pon must deliver packages to its inhabitants, and often lend a paw to their predicaments.
Oh, and Pon's also a BMX enthusiast, which means that he can take advantage of the landscape's many bike ramps and grinding rails to get around more (or less) efficiently.
There's a whole trick system that you can master, and while far from mandatory, pulling off sick moves as you go about your business nets you extra money at the end of your shift. Additional moolah lets you purchase more decorations for your shrine — which you're free to customise when you're not at work.
The relaxed process of cycling around the island, meeting quirky new characters, and taking part in an impressive variety of minigames — like fishing, bug catching, pint pouring, sushi stacking, and many others — is surprisingly moreish.
Indeed, developer Denkiworks has created something quite special in terms of structure. It feels like the game's always coming up with clever new ways to keep you entertained, which makes for a very nicely paced package.
That said, a few of the minigames can come across as slightly tedious. Picking up trash or sanding the bark off logs, for example, can't compare with landing a big fish, or partaking in a spot of sumo. Still, as alluded, it's hard to fault the variety that's on offer.
Lovingly put together and full of heart, Tanuki: Pon's Summer is a fantastic little slice of relaxation.
Robert (or Rob if you're lazy) is an assistant editor of Push Square, and has been a fan of PlayStation since the 90s, when Tekken 2 introduced him to the incredible world of video games. He still takes his fighting games seriously, but RPGs are his true passion. The Witcher, Persona, Dragon Quest, Mass Effect, Final Fantasy, Trails, Tales — he's played 'em all. A little too much, some might say.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine
Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.
A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.
The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea , Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.
Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.
In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”
Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.
In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.
Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin.
The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.
after newsletter promotion
Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.
Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , said on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including towns and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.
Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he said, citing conversations with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

articles.title_orig: Intel claims its 350W D270 GPU is up to 5.9x faster than NVIDIA's 600W RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell
articles.title_zh: Intel claims its 350W D270 GPU is up to 5.9x faster than NVIDIA's 600W RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell
articles.content_orig:
Intel has published GPU D270 benchmarks comparing its Xe3P accelerator against NVIDIA Blackwell.
Intel has published new performance results for its GPU D270, previously known as Crescent Island. The company claims its 350W accelerator delivers up to 5.9 times higher application throughput than NVIDIA’s RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition in selected financial computing workloads. The results come from Intel’s internal testing using pre-production hardware.
The D270 is based on Intel’s Xe3P architecture, featuring 32 Xe cores and 256 XMX engines. The Intel-branded card has 160GB of LPDDR5X memory with 1.5 TB/s of bandwidth, while partner configurations can support up to 480GB. For comparison, NVIDIA’s RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition has 96GB of GDDR7 memory and up to 600W power consumption. Intel’s card is designed for a 350W power limit.
Intel’s largest performance advantage comes from financial applications using double-precision FP64 calculations. According to the company’s results, the D270 delivers between 1.92x and 5.9x the application throughput of NVIDIA’s GPU, depending on the workload.
These results are closely related to the hardware’s FP64 capabilities. Intel’s Xe3P architecture supports native FP64 operations with 64 fused multiply-add operations per Xe core. NVIDIA’s RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell is designed primarily for professional graphics and AI computing, rather than maximum FP64 throughput. The comparison therefore favors Intel’s architecture in workloads that depend on double-precision calculations.
Intel also published AI inference comparisons using the same NVIDIA accelerator. In Qwen3-30B-A3B FP8 testing, the D270 delivered 1.12x the throughput of the RTX PRO 6000. In Drex 2.0 testing, Intel reported 29% lower latency. Both comparisons used single GPUs, although the test platforms and software configurations differed.
Intel’s financial benchmark appendix lists a system containing one D270 and three Arc Pro B70 cards, while the NVIDIA test system contained eight RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. It does not clearly explain the active GPU allocation for each financial workload
Intel is also working with SambaNova on a disaggregated AI inference platform combining D270 GPUs for prompt processing with SN50 accelerators for token generation. The company plans to demonstrate the configuration at SC26. Intel has not announced general availability dates or pricing for the D270.

articles.title_orig: Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
articles.title_zh: Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
articles.content_orig:
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 .
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries .
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

articles.title_orig: New Data Paves the Way for Weight-Loss Drugs for Young Children, but Questions Remain
articles.title_zh: New Data Paves the Way for Weight-Loss Drugs for Young Children, but Questions Remain
articles.content_orig:
New results from a closely watched clinical trial showed that weight-loss drugs are effective for children as young as 6, though some doctors say they are concerned about the prospect of prescribing these medications to such young patients.
The study, presented Monday at the medical conference Obesity Week, examined children ages 6 to 11 who were taking semaglutide, the compound in Ozempic and Wegovy. Most children in the trial had severe obesity, meaning they had a body mass index of 35 or higher. After 68 weeks, nearly 40 percent of those who took the drug no longer had obesity, compared with none of the patients on a placebo.
Novo Nordisk, the drug’s maker, said it would ask the Food and Drug Administration to approve the medication for this age group. The drug is already authorized for children 12 and over. Another new study, also presented at the conference, showed that the weight-loss drug tirzepatide was effective in children age 12 and older.
Doctors widely agree that more needs to be done to address obesity, which affects roughly one in five children and adolescents nationwide. But they are divided over whether powerful GLP-1 drugs, which rewire the brain’s relationship to food, are the right approach. Some are concerned about the potential long-term implications of putting children who are still growing on a drug that erases appetite and can lead people to consume very few calories.
In October, the World Health Organization cautioned against using weight-loss drugs in children under 10, citing a lack of evidence on their effects on children’s growth, development and mental health.
“The question is: Is this the right thing to do?” said Dr. Robert Lustig, a professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco. “Not, does it work? Of course it works. But is it the right thing?”

articles.title_orig: U.K. considers changing laws on age for sexual consent in wake of Russell Brand case
articles.title_zh: U.K. considers changing laws on age for sexual consent in wake of Russell Brand case
articles.content_orig:
London —  Britain's government is considering changing the U.K.'s laws on the legal age of sexual consent as a woman who claims she was raped by convicted sex offender Russell Brand campaigns to criminalize sex between adults and 16- or 17-year-olds.
British Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said over the weekend that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" had emerged last week, warranting consideration of a new law that would set out different ages of consent depending on the ages of the individuals involved.
Already practiced by several other nations, the merits of this staggered age of consent approach have "been raised and will be discussed" by the government, McFadden said, adding that he "can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."
A day after Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault , fellow British television personality and author David Walliams was named as the subject of multiple allegations of grooming young girls and harassing female colleagues .
Under current U.K. law, an adult of any age can have sex with a consenting person 16 years old or older. If a staggered system were imposed, it could make it illegal for anyone 18 or older, for instance, to have sex with individuals aged between 16 and 18, regardless of whether they gave verbal consent.
There is plenty of precedent: In eight U.S. states —   Idaho, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, North Dakota and Florida, where Brand was living before he was jailed — the age of consent varies depending on the age gap between the two people .
In Idaho, for example, if one person is under 16 and the other is 18 or older, or if the victim is 16 or 17 years old and the perpetrator is at least three years older, it is classed as rape. "Lewd contact with a child" younger than 16 is a crime regardless of the perpetrator's age.
In most U.S. states, the age of consent has a "close-in-age" exception for people under 18 who engage in mutually consentual sexual acts.
In Canada, where the age of consent is 16, the staggered-age system includes more detailed , age-dependent exemptions. For people aged 12-13, the partner must be less than two years older; age 14-15, the partner must be less than five years older, and between 16-17, people are generally seen as able to give consent, unless their sexual partner is in a position of trust or authority toward them.
Austria, Belgium, France, Ireland and South Africa also have close-in-age exemptions.
Mia Latter, now 37, has accused Brand of raping her when she was 16 and he was 30, and she is now campaigning for a staggered age of consent to be introduced in Britain.
Latter, whose allegations were not part of the case that saw Brand convicted last week of raping and sexually assaulting other women, abandoned her anonymity as an accuser of the celebrity in an interview published over the weekend by The Sunday Times . She told the newspaper she was speaking out to help "protect teenagers from being groomed by older men or women."
"I don't want to criminalize teenagers having sex with each other," she said. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offense."
Brand protested his innocence from jail on Sunday in a statement read out by his wife Laura.
The prime minister's office said Monday that the comments were under investigation, as "prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

articles.title_orig: Fed chair Kevin Warsh says AI boom could help sustain ‘substantially higher’ US growth
articles.title_zh: Fed chair Kevin Warsh says AI boom could help sustain ‘substantially higher’ US growth
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields dipped on Monday as the stock market retreated and Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh warned that artificial intelligence might "disppoint."
The 10-year Treasury yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, loans and credit card debt — fell 3.2 basis points, to 5.119% after reaching a high of 5.174% on Friday.
The 2-year Treasury note yield , more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was off by more than 5 basis points, to 4.821%. The 30-year Treasury bond yield was down a little more than 1 basis point, at 5.468%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Warsh spoke in San Francisco on the impact of technology on productivity and jobs on Monday, telling a blue-ribbon task force he assembled that that there could be "less positive" outcomes from artificial intelligence, including job displacement that could increase unemployment. Another possibility is simply that AI could just "disappoint."
Another possibility is that AI enhances productivity and proves disinflationary, Warsha said.
Either way, AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road," the central bank leader said.
Warsh's remarks came after data last week showed the annual rate of increase in the producer price index stood at 6.5% in October, the highest in almost four years. Expectations that cost pressures could be passed along to consumers, further fueling inflation, intensified pressure and contributed to a sell-off in  Treasurys last week.
October's retail sales, due for release at 8:30 a.m. ET Tuesday, will give traders another update on the economy and the state of consumer spending.
Economists expect retail sales grew 0.6% in October, les than September's 0.8% rise. September's strength was in large part due to a 6.4% increase in gasoline sales on the back of higher prices.
The Federal Reserve's minutes from its October meeting, where it left rates unchanged, will be released Wednesday. Markets have largely priced in a quarter percentage point hike in December, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
— With additional reporting by CNBC's Jeff Cox

articles.title_orig: Trump says he might meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
articles.title_zh: Trump says he might meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
articles.content_orig:
Trump's trip comes amid the Nvidia CEO scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As he departed the White House Monday morning, Trump said he "may" meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China as well, though he said it would ultimately be Xi's decision.
"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump said of Kim Jong Un.
Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China.
An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump is expected to leave Washington in the morning of Monday, Nov. 16 and arrive in Manila in the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17, and will head to a bilateral meeting with the other members of the Quad, a diplomatic partnership the U.S. has with Australia, India, and Japan, about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.
He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. He will also participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi.
The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing.
Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics.
When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott.
Now, in the background of this trip, is the scandal involving Nvidia's CEO, Huang, who joined Trump's last trip to China earlier this year after boarding Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, according to pool reports at the time. Huang was reported to have had an affair with Alice Huang , a Chinese national and tech executive who is accused of being a Chinese spy.
Officials said they do not expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, with President Xi, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12.
This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy.
"Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9.
When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had."
On May 12, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the plot. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said.
A U.S. official and a source familiar with the matter told ABC News that after Air Force One landed in China, White House officials asked for business leaders -- including Huang -- to be allowed into a meeting with President Xi. Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi.
Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months.
For example, the U.S. has long blocked China's access to American AI chips. However, in December 2025, after lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened those restrictions -- approving the sale of some older but still powerful chips to China as part of a remarkable deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of the sales.
And in July of this year, Huang joined the social media platform X to push back against possible bans on open-weight AI models, the type that Chinese companies have embraced, and which would be cheaper for businesses and governments to adopt. The ban would benefit American companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which use closed models. The U.S. was reportedly considering those bans.
"The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models," Huang wrote in his first-ever X post.
This trip marks Trump's first one overseas since American voters handed him and Republicans a devastating defeat in the midterm elections. Voter Polls show voters rejected the president’s tariffs and the war in Iran -- two of Trump's key foreign policy positions.

articles.title_orig: China has ‘normalized’ naval presence near Japan since political spat of 2025
articles.title_zh: China has ‘normalized’ naval presence near Japan since political spat of 2025
articles.content_orig:
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — In early November, Taiwan’s National Security Council secretary-general tracked more than 100 Chinese military-linked vessels near his island.
But given its scale, the massive flotilla that included coast guard vessels alongside navy warships may have had Taiwan’s maritime neighbor Japan in its sights, military experts say.
They say China has sent an outsized number of its far-seas naval deployments to near Japan’s southernmost islands and nearby waters since a political dispute that erupted in November 2025 over a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Takaichi told a Japanese House of Representatives committee session that month that a Chinese naval blockade or armed conflict involving Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for her own country not far away. China claims self-ruled Taiwan as its own and has not ruled out the use of force to take it.
“There is a direct link between Takaichi’s statement and the quality and quantity of deployments,” said Stephen Nagy, a visiting fellow with the Japan Institute for International Affairs think tank in Tokyo. “(China) is also sending a signal to Tokyo that if it continues its current position vis-a-vis Taiwan that Beijing will continue these activities.”
China is using the deployments, including live-fire drills, uncrewed drone missions and voyages by entire aircraft carrier groups, to exert an unrelenting, long-term pressure on Japan without violating international maritime laws, analysts said.
“By repeatedly transiting waters around the (southwestern) Islands, China is gradually normalizing PLA Navy activity within the first island chain, expanding its operational experience and creating a pattern of accepted presence,” said Katsuya Yamamoto, director of the Tokyo-based Sasakawa Peace Foundation’s strategy and deterrence program.
The first island chain includes Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines.
“In other words, it is establishing facts on the ground, or rather at sea, that broaden its future freedom of action,” Yamamoto said.
In the seven weeks after Takaichi’s comment, the U.S. think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies logged a spike in “notable” PLA escalatory moves. Over 2025 overall, it said, China showed just a “slight increase” in the number of PLA naval vessels reported operating in waters around Japan, including an increase in the number of Chinese ships within the contiguous zone of the disputed Senkaku Islands, which China calls the Diaoyu.
Deployments near the uninhabited, Japanese-controlled Senkakus have “remained at very high levels” over the past year as before, while joint Sino-Russian missions around Japan and Chinese naval activity near the outlying Japanese islets around the Miyako Island “seem to have increased”, said Jeffrey Kingston, a professor specializing in Asian studies and history at Temple University, Japan Campus.
Chinese and Russian aircraft patrolled in June over the Sea of Japan, followed by a joint naval passage in July in the Miyako Strait near outlying Japanese islets. Chinese and Russian surveillance aircraft did five separate flights near Japan in October.
Spokespeople for the Chinese ministries of foreign affairs and national defense have called China’s military actions fair, valid and peaceful.
China is probably using military moves as one in a series of measures – some economic – to get back at Takaichi for her November 2025 remarks, Kingston said. “They haven’t forgotten, that’s for sure,” he said. “They are in various ways trying to put the screws on her.”
Officials in Beijing still want a retraction of the prime minister’s November 2025 comments but it’s unlikely, Kingston believes.
The Japanese government has verbally protested against Chinese military moves, tracked Chinese ships with its own, and scrambled fighter jets.
Tokyo is now considering a 70 trillion to 80 trillion yen (as high as $508 billion) defense spending plan for the five-year period beginning in April 2027, up from 43 trillion yen in the previous half-decade span, Japanese media outlets have reported.
“As the security environment becomes increasingly severe, cooperation with the ally and like-minded countries is indispensable to peace and stability in the region,” Japan’s Ministry of Defense said in an Oct. 29 statement after a meeting with defense officials from Australia, the Philippines and the United States.
The ministry, it said, “will continue to take advantage of various opportunities to further strengthen such cooperation.”

articles.title_orig: Permitting Bill Would Charge Data Centers Billions for Power
articles.title_zh: Permitting Bill Would Charge Data Centers Billions for Power
articles.content_orig:
Weeks after voters lashed out at data centers in the midterms, Congress is debating a sweeping overhaul of federal permitting rules that could help tech companies more quickly build the facilities.
The bill would speed up federal environmental reviews of a variety of energy projects, including transmission lines and gas pipelines, making it easier for developers to get the power they need to run data centers.
But that help comes with a huge catch: Data centers would also have to pay much more for their electricity under a provision in the bill that would charge the facilities extra for access to the electric grid. That measure would upend decades of federal power rules and potentially save billions of dollars over the next decade for households and other ratepayers.
The push to impose higher costs on data centers underscores how thorny the politics around A.I. have become in Washington. Massive, energy-hungry data centers are spreading rapidly across the country, straining electrical networks and triggering anger in many communities . Voters this month approved at least 40 local ballot initiatives to restrict the facilities.
Some environmentalists who oppose the permitting bill have cast it as a boon to tech companies, arguing that the legislation could accelerate the development of data centers powered by natural gas. The bill would pare back federal environmental laws to speed construction of many types of projects, including gas pipelines, wind and solar projects, high-voltage transmission lines, roads, public transit and housing.

articles.title_orig: To Stop Iran’s Rearmament, Trump Must Confront Russia and China
articles.title_zh: To Stop Iran’s Rearmament, Trump Must Confront Russia and China
articles.content_orig:
Click here to download the JINSA Insight
At the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18–19, President Donald Trump expects to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the summit’s sidelines to discuss getting their assistance in ending the war in Iran, while their two countries are helping sustain Tehran’s war effort. Yet, while the Trump administration has intensified military and economic pressure on Iran, it has simultaneously granted sanctions relief to Russia and refrained from targeting major Chinese financial institutions facilitating Iran’s illicit oil trade.
This contradictory approach risks leaving intact the foreign networks that could finance and rebuild Iran’s postwar rearmament in the event of an accord, as Chinese supplies helped Iran rebuild after the June 2025 12-Day War. Washington must confront the countries enabling Iran’s military recovery, and Shenzhen offers the perfect setting to do so.
Pressure on Iran, Relief for Its Backers
Since the United States and Israel launched Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion against Iran on February 28, the Trump administration has executed successive campaigns against Tehran’s revenue streams, procurement networks, and smuggling routes. The U.S. naval blockade, first implemented on April 13 and reimposed on July 14, has prevented, according to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Iran from earning more than $25 billion in crude oil revenue. The Treasury Department’s Operation Economic Fury , launched in April, targeted the financing infrastructure providing the basis for Iran’s trade and shadow-banking networks. In August, Operation Economic Outcast , or Economic “D-Day,” extended pressure on Tehran’s foreign financial enablers through sanctions and warning of secondary sanctions measures. The most recent initiative, CENTCOM’s Task Force Iron Gate , coordinates efforts against illicit shipments and revenue flows across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea, routes the regime has increasingly utilized because of the U.S. blockade.
Despite these initiatives to go after Iran, Washington has pursued competing policies toward the Islamic Republic’s two primary foreign backers. The administration first provided sanctions waivers on Russian seaborne oil in March, a waiver which it extended twice, allowing Moscow to continue earning revenue from sanctioned oil shipments until the relief ultimately expired in June. In October, the administration authorized temporary transactions for Russian diesel until April 2027 and waived multiple provisions included in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The White House justified the Graham Act waivers by saying enforcing the sanctions provisions “would impede ongoing US efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia.”
Washington has equally shied away from imposing its most consequential financial penalties on China. While the Treasury has imposed sanctions on China’s independent “teapot” oil refineries, Hong Kong-based intermediaries , and procurement companies enabling Iranian trade, it has stopped short of targeting the broader Chinese financial networks that facilitate Iranian oil payments and move the proceeds into the international financial system. When Xi visited Trump in September at the White House, the two extended their trade truce but reached no agreement on Chinese support for Tehran. The administration appears, therefore, reluctant to make any move jeopardizing U.S.-China economic relations even as it attempts to sever Iran’s foreign financial lifelines.
Russia’s Role in Arming Iran
Russia serves as one of Iran’s most consequential military and intelligence suppliers, helping Tehran lead operations against U.S. forces and regional partners. Since March, Moscow has, according to open-source reporting, provided upgraded Geran-2 attack drones , explosives , satellite imagery , and targeting intelligence that bolstered Iranian capabilities during the war. Reports also indicate that Russia is assisting Iran in developing advanced cruise missiles , which would strengthen Tehran’s ability to penetrate regional air defenses. Russia is equally aiding Iran’s strategy of using its proxy network to open a two-front war, as Moscow is reportedly sharing intelligence with the Houthis to carry out attacks on Red Sea shipping.
Russia’s assistance could become even more consequential after a cessation of hostilities. According to The Telegraph , Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, delivered a November 5 letter from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei requesting Russian S-400 air defense systems. Tehran has also pursued Russia’s 4.5-generation Su-35 fighters and will reportedly receive them following the war’s conclusion . A prewar Iranian parliamentary memorandum also obtained by The Telegraph outlined plans to deepen cooperation with Moscow on missiles, drones, and air defenses, suggesting that Tehran views foreign military assistance, especially that from Russia, as a central pillar of its long-term survival. Of course, Russia’s war in Ukraine limits what weaponry it can spare to its Iranian partner, but even selective transfers of air defense components and drone technology would raise the cost of future U.S. or Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear and missile facilities.
China’s Role in Financing Iran’s Recovery
China has been more cautious than Russia about transferring complete weapons systems during the ongoing war, but it has played perhaps the largest role in financing Iran’s reconstruction through oil purchases and providing critical components for weapons systems to operate. According to prewar statistics, Beijing bought about 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil exports through independent teapot refineries, making it responsible for an estimated 45 percent of Iran’s total government budget. Iran’s reliance on China has continued during the war, with Kpler data identifying Beijing as the only purchaser of Iranian crude in October. On the weapons front, Chinese firms have supplied Iran with the crucial missile propellant precursor sodium perchlorate , as well as dual-use drone components . The full extent of direct Chinese military assistance during the current war remains uncertain, but the presence of these procurement networks could again accelerate Tehran’s rearmament should hostilities end.
Iran is reportedly constructing more durable infrastructure in China aimed at circumventing U.S. sanctions. According to a recent Iran International report , citing a leaked letter from Iran’s Oil Ministry, Iran now controls a terminal in the Ningbo-Zhoushan free trade zone, holds stakes in docks in Shandong province, and owns seven storage tanks in Dalian, Huizhou, Dongying, Weifang, and Zhoushan. This infrastructure allows tankers in the fleet of Hossein Shamkhani, son of the late Khamenei adviser Ali Shamkhani, 51 of whose vessels the Treasury has sanctioned, to unload near refinery pipelines and allows Iran to store its crude in China before securing buyers, which mitigates the impact of existing Treasury designations and suggests that Iran is building sanctions-resistant oil facilities in China with Beijing’s tacit approval or acquiescence.
The Precedent of the 12-Day War
Iran’s recovery in the wake of previous U.S. and Israeli air campaigns against it is a case in point as to why battlefield success alone cannot guarantee lasting strategic gains. Israel’s October 2024 strikes on Iran reportedly decreased Tehran’s capacity to produce solid fuel for ballistic missiles by approximately 93 percent, from enough for 14 missiles per week to just one. Eight months later, operations during the 12-Day War destroyed additional missile production facilities, launchers, and stockpiles, again reducing Iran’s operational arsenal. articles.title_orig: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’
articles.title_zh: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’
articles.content_orig:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

articles.title_orig: Gemini rolling out 66 new regional voices on Android and iOS, including 10+ UK dialects
articles.title_zh: Gemini rolling out 66 new regional voices on Android and iOS, including 10+ UK dialects
articles.content_orig:
Following a preview at Google I/O , Google is rolling out 66 new regional voices to the Gemini app on both Android and iOS today. The expansion introduces tailored voice options across U.S. English, U.K. English, Indian English, Hindi, Brazilian Portuguese, Indonesian, and Korean.
For users in the UK, the update brings over 10 distinct English voice options covering a wide range of regional cadences. The lineup includes Geordie, Scouse, Brummie, Scottish, Welsh, Northern Irish, Modern RP, and Multicultural London English (MLE).
This might help reduce the issues that sometimes still occur when English accents , in particular, morph into a hybrid of Australian or even American that has been going on for a while with Gemini Live. We have not yet been able to test to confirm this has been resolved with the update. As someone with a regional English accent, this extra representation with Gemini voices is quite welcome.
According to Google, these voices are tuned for natural pronunciation, pitch, and everyday local rhythm rather than exaggerated stereotypes. Because the focus is on cadence over slang, Gemini will sound like a local without filling its text responses with forced street slang. Once selected, your chosen voice carries across the entire app, applying to both Gemini Live conversations and standard text-to-speech playback when tapping the “Listen” icon on chat responses.
You can preview and select the new options today by tapping the three-dot menu inside Gemini Live, or by heading into the Gemini app settings and selecting “Gemini’s voice.” It’s worth noting that the voices aren’t explicitly labeled by city or region in the app menu, and Gemini isn’t programmed to self-identify which accent it is using if you ask it directly.
Instead, Google notes that locally rooted prompts about food, culture, or sport, such as asking for the best pub in Sheffield for a Sunday roast – my suggestion is not a pub; it’s Turnip & Thyme on Eccleshall Road, FWIW. Or another suggestion from big G is where to find proper ingredients for a traditional Scouse stew; the company says these will naturally bring out the warmth and rhythm of the new dialects.
I’d suggest trying to ask where to get the best pattie and chips in Hull or where to get the best pint in Leeds (it’s Whitelocks).
